transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Yeah, thanks. I suppose the main thing is that I’m having a really hard time staying with things that I actually need to do. I’m a secondary school teacher, and a lot of my work involves sitting down with essays to mark, or reading through curriculum documents, planning materials, that sort of thing. I’ll sit down fully intending to get through it — like, I’ll have the pile in front of me, I’ll have made a cup of tea, I’ll tell myself, “Right, I’m doing this now” — and then after maybe ten minutes I realize I’ve been staring at the same page and almost nothing has gone in.

It’s not that I don’t care about it. That’s the frustrating part. I’ll be looking at a student’s essay or some document I genuinely need to understand, and my mind has gone off in three different directions at once. I’ll be thinking about something from earlier in the day, or something I need to do later, or just some completely unrelated thought, and then I sort of come back and realize I’ve been reading the same paragraph over and over without taking it in.

That’s really what brought me here — it’s starting to feel like I can’t rely on my attention when I need it.
Have you noticed these difficulties with concentration and staying focused in other parts of your life, like at home or in social situations, or does it seem to only happen when you're working?

No, it’s definitely not just work. Work is where it causes the biggest obvious problems, because there’s paperwork and meetings and deadlines, but I notice it at home as well.

Like, in planning meetings at school, I’ll be sitting there looking at whoever’s speaking, and I’m nodding along, and from the outside I probably look like I’m listening properly. But then someone will say, “What do you think about that?” or ask me to respond to the actual point they’ve just made, and I realise I’ve missed the middle of it, or sometimes the main point entirely. And then I’m trying to piece it together from context, which is quite embarrassing.

It happens with my wife too. She’ll be telling me something at home — not even anything boring necessarily, just normal conversation — and I’m looking right at her, but my attention sort of slips. Then she’ll ask what I think, or expect me to answer, and I haven’t properly taken in what she’s just said. I feel awful about that because it can seem like I’m not interested or I don’t care, and that’s not how it feels from my side. It’s more like I’m there physically, and I’m trying to listen, but the actual content doesn’t always land.
Have you ever felt restless or found yourself needing to be constantly moving, like you can't sit still for very long, even if you're trying to focus on something important?

I’m not sure, really. I wouldn’t say that’s the main thing I’ve noticed. I mean, I can get a bit uncomfortable sitting for ages, like anyone would, especially in a long meeting or if I’ve been at my desk too long, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as needing to constantly move or feeling like I physically can’t sit still.

It’s more that my mind goes off somewhere, if that makes sense, rather than my body. I might shift around in my chair or get up to make tea, but I’ve never really thought of myself as especially restless in that way. So… no, not particularly, or at least not something that’s stood out to me as a major problem.
Have you ever found yourself acting without thinking, like interrupting others, making impulsive decisions, or feeling like you need to jump into things quickly without considering the consequences?

I’m not sure, to be honest. I wouldn’t immediately think of myself as someone who acts without thinking in that way. I mean, I’m sure I’ve interrupted people occasionally — especially if I’m worried I’ll forget what I was going to say — but I don’t know that it’s a pattern, or not one that jumps out at me as a big issue.

With decisions, I’m probably more likely to overthink than suddenly do something reckless. I don’t really feel like I’m constantly jumping into things without considering what might happen. If anything, I tend to get stuck trying to work out what I’m meant to be doing or what the best order is.

So… no, I wouldn’t say impulsiveness is something I’ve particularly noticed. At least, not compared with the concentration side of things.
Have you ever felt an inner sense of restlessness or found it hard to relax, even when you’re not particularly stressed or busy?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I do find it hard to switch off sometimes, but I’ve always put that down to normal life things — thinking about work, things at home, whatever needs doing the next day. I don’t really recognise an inner restlessness as such, not in the sense of feeling driven or unable to relax for no clear reason.

If I’m sitting at home in the evening, I can relax physically. I’m not pacing around or feeling like I have to be doing something constantly. Sometimes I might feel a bit unsettled if I know there are things I haven’t sorted, but that feels more like worry or mental clutter than restlessness. So… I don’t think so. It’s not something that stands out to me as a problem.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy, even a little bit, over the past couple of weeks?

I don’t think so, no. Not in a way that I’d describe as feeling hopeless or properly down. I mean, everyone has flat days, don’t they, especially if work’s been a lot or I’ve had a frustrating day, but over the past couple of weeks I wouldn’t say I’ve been persistently low.

And I don’t think I’ve lost interest in things I normally enjoy either. Sometimes I don’t get round to doing them, or I’ll put things off and then feel annoyed with myself, but that’s not really the same as not enjoying them. If I actually sit down to watch something I like or see people or do something relaxing, I can still enjoy it.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed that. I wouldn’t say hopeless, and I don’t think there’s been a loss of pleasure.
Looking back, were you someone who had a lot of energy as a child, or did people ever tell you that you had trouble sitting still or staying focused on tasks when you were growing up?

Yeah, I think the “staying focused on tasks” part fits more than the “lots of energy” bit. I don’t remember being especially hyper or the kind of child who was constantly running around, but school reports are where it showed up, I think.

Even in primary school, I’d get comments along the lines of, you know, “bright but careless,” or “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” That sort of thing came up more than once, from what I remember and from what my parents used to say. It wasn’t that I couldn’t understand the work — apparently I could do it when someone was sitting with me or checking in — but if I was left to get on with it, I’d drift or miss bits or just not finish.

And my parents were always finding worksheets in my backpack, all crumpled up, that I’d done or half-done and then just forgotten to hand in. I can still remember that awful feeling of them pulling out some sheet that should have been turned in days before, and me not even having a good explanation. It wasn’t deliberate, I just… it vanished from my mind once it was in the bag, I suppose. So yes, looking back, there were definitely signs like that, even quite early on.
Can you think of any other situations or environments, besides work and home, where you’ve noticed these issues with staying focused or keeping your attention where it needs to be?

Yes… the main one that comes to mind is school, but not just “work” in the general sense — specifically marking or reading documents. That’s actually a big part of why I came in, to be honest.

I can sit down with a stack of essays, or a curriculum document, and I’m fully intending to get through it. I’ll have made the time, I’ll have the papers in front of me, sometimes I’ll even have a pen in my hand ready to start making notes. And then within, I don’t know, ten minutes, I suddenly realise I’ve been staring at the same page and I haven’t really taken in what I’ve read. My eyes have gone over the words, but my mind has been somewhere completely different — thinking about three other things, or replaying something from earlier, or jumping ahead to what I need to do next.

It’s frustrating because it’s not that I don’t care or that I’m trying to avoid it. I’ll sit there with every intention of doing it properly, and then I sort of come to and realise I’ve barely moved on. Sometimes I have to reread the same paragraph several times because I know technically I’ve “read” it, but none of it has actually stuck. That happens with longer documents especially, but even with essays it can happen if I’m meant to sustain attention for a while.
As a child, did you ever feel restless or find it hard to stay still, even when you knew you were supposed to?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I don’t remember being particularly restless in that physical sense, like not being able to stay in my seat or constantly needing to move around. That doesn’t really stand out to me from childhood.

I mean, I’m sure I fidgeted sometimes — most children do, don’t they? — but I don’t have a strong memory of teachers telling me off for getting up when I shouldn’t, or my parents saying I was impossible to keep still. If anything, the things I remember more are around not staying with a task mentally rather than feeling like my body had to be moving.

So… no, I wouldn’t confidently say that was a big thing for me. It may have happened a bit, but it’s not something I particularly remember as a problem.
